# Unclaimed

Twenty-two years behind the glass at the Lost Property Office, Platform One, and I can tell you this: nobody comes back for an umbrella.

They come back for glasses, always. For medication, within the hour, white-faced, patting every pocket. For laptops, phones, passports — they arrive breathless before the train has even finished pulling away. But umbrellas, never. We have four hundred and eleven of them in the rack downstairs, and I have counted twice, because counting them is the sort of thing you do when the platform goes quiet. Black ones, mostly. One shaped like a parrot. They stand there in the dark like a little forest of things people meant to care about and didn't. You'd think rain would help. It's the opposite — rain just makes people buy new ones, and the rack grows.

The work is cataloguing. Everything gets a number, a date, a shelf. A violin case with no violin inside it — number 88-114, unclaimed, eleven years now. A wedding dress, boxed, slightly crushed, smelling faintly of somebody else's smoke. A single leather shoe, men's, size nine, polished so lovingly that I walked the whole train myself looking for its twin. A paper bag of children's drawings, crayon suns and stick-figure dogs, left by a woman who cried at the window describing them and then, when I found them, decided she couldn't afford the storage fee and left them anyway. I did not charge her. There is no storage fee. There never has been. I just wanted to hear what she'd say.

A set of dentures in a napkin. A trombone. Once, a live ferret in a carrier, which is another story entirely, involving the stationmaster and a great deal of shouting.

People are strange about objects. They'll surrender a phone — a phone — and fight me over a paperback with a cracked spine. A man once left a briefcase containing eleven thousand pounds in cash and returned two days later, calm as Sunday, signing for it without counting. Another time a soldier's duffel bag sat unclaimed for a full season, and when he finally came — bigger than I'd pictured, walking differently than soldiers walk in films — he stood holding it in the doorway a long while before he could speak. He said, "I wasn't sure I was coming back for it." He didn't say where he'd been. He didn't have to. Some bags you can hear the weight of.

The rule is ninety days. After ninety days, unclaimed items go to the charity shop down the road, or the bin, depending. Glasses to the optician, clothes to the shop, books to whoever wants them. It's a good rule. Without it the place would fill up and drown, shelf by shelf, until we were nothing but a museum of other people's forgetting.

But there are items I have held past the ninety days. Don't tell anyone. There's a hearing aid that's been here four months because I cannot make myself send it away — somewhere there's an old man leaning toward conversations, nodding at guesses. And there was the urn.

A woman left an urn on the 6:42, on the luggage rack, wrapped in a scarf. Her mother, it turned out. She'd been moving house — moving the mother from one mantelpiece to another — and somewhere between stations she'd set the bag down and stood up too early, the way you do, and walked off into her new life without her old one. She came back three days later, grey as paper. By then it had been catalogued — number, date, shelf — and I want you to understand what that felt like, typing a dead woman into a spreadsheet. MRS. E. HOLLOWAY. CONTENTS: ASHES. I kept her at my desk, not on the shelf, for those three days. When the daughter came I carried her out myself, both hands, like something hot. The daughter said thank you eleven times. I counted that too.

Here's what nobody tells you about a lost property office: it isn't a room of lost things. It's a room of interrupted sentences. Every object is a clause somebody didn't finish. The umbrella is *I'll only need it this morning*. The violin case — empty, mind you, empty — is a whole symphony of questions I've stopped asking.

And then there's the thing I kept.

Ninety days is a long time to know an object. You turn it over, you read it, sometimes it reads you. Years ago — my fourth year, I think — a brown coat came in, size large, mothed at the cuffs, and in the pocket was a folded note in pencil, soft with handling, the way notes get when they're written fast and read often. It said: *Gone to get milk. Back by six.* And underneath, smaller: *don't wait up if I'm late — love you either way.*

No name. No date. The coat was never claimed. Ninety days, then the shop, per the rule. But the note — the note went into my breast pocket, and it has been in one breast pocket or another ever since, twenty-odd years, moved coat to coat like a pilot light.

Because here's what I know: somewhere, someone wrote that and meant it. Someone was coming back by six. Maybe they did. Maybe they didn't. The note doesn't say, and that's the mercy of it. As long as it stays unread by history, unsolved, the promise is still standing. Somewhere it is always five minutes to six, and someone is walking home with milk in a bag, and the kitchen light is on, and everything is still about to happen.

I retire in the spring. They asked if I'd like to take anything from the office as a keepsake. Four hundred and twelve umbrellas, a violin case, a parrot.

I took the note. It was mine already. Some things aren't lost. They're just waiting for the right pocket.
